title: Complete nested cross-validation outputs for reliable model validation under class imbalance
abstract: Complete derived computational outputs accompanying the study “Practical Guidelines for Permutation-Based Model Validation in Machine Learning under Class Imbalance”. The archive contains the full nested cross-validation and permutation-testing outputs for the FP and FPs problem formulations across AdaBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, and XGBoost. It includes observed-label runs, 720 permutation runs, out-of-fold predictions, fold-level results, selected-feature records, ROC data, and run summaries. The raw aero-engine observations are not included in this deposit. The target_index field in the out-of-fold prediction files is an internally generated zero-based positional index used by the outer cross-validation procedure and is not an original dataset identifier. The source code and reproducibility workflow are archived separately on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23348132.

title: Classical capacity of squeezed-noise channels: optimal photon allocation without entangled encoding
abstract: Directional optical noise makes photons pay for both squeezing and signal modulation. This paper determines the optimal transmitter and the ultimate classical communication rate, even when arbitrary entangled and non-Gaussian encodings across many channel uses are allowed. For a finite collection of independent squeezed thermal attenuators with different losses and noise covariances, the complete quantum optimization reduces exactly to a scalar allocation of the total mean photon budget. The result covers every input energy, including the low-energy regime in which only one quadrature should be modulated, channels receiving zero photons, and pure squeezed environments. 1. Exact capacity and all-block additivity. Let \(\Phi=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{d}\Phi_j\), let \(E\ge0\) be the total average input photon number per block, and let \(C_j(E_j)\) be the explicitly attained one-channel rate specified in the paper. Then \[ C(\Phi,E)=\chi_\Phi(E)=\max_{E_j\ge0,\,\sum_jE_j\le E}\sum_{j=1}^{d} C_j(E_j), \] \[ \chi_{\Phi^{\otimes n}}(nE)=nC(\Phi,E)\qquad(n\ge1). \] The optimization includes arbitrary joint input ensembles, with an average physical photon constraint and unrestricted decoding. Independent Gaussian modulation of pure squeezed states attains the answer. Thus neither non-Gaussian codewords nor entanglement across the specified independent channels or repeated blocks improves the capacity. Information quantities use natural logarithms; division by \(\ln2\) gives bits. 2. From measured channel noise to a transmitter design. In quadratures with vacuum covariance \(I/2\), each channel acts as \(V\mapsto\eta V+\operatorname{diag}(y_q,y_p)\), where \(0<\eta<1\), \(y_q\ge y_p>0\), and \(y_qy_p\ge(1-\eta)^2/4\). Define \[ u_e=\frac12\sqrt{\frac{y_q}{y_p}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{th}}=u_e-\frac12+\frac{y_q-y_p}{2\eta}. \] Below this threshold, a bounded one-dimensional maximization determines the optimal seed squeezing and the modulation of the quieter quadrature. Above it, both quadratures can be modulated and the average output is isotropic. Writing \(g(x)=(x+1)\ln(x+1)-x\ln x\), the high-energy rate is \[ C_j(E)=g\!\left(\eta E+\frac{\eta+y_q+y_p-1}{2}\right)-g\!\left(\frac{\eta}{2}+\sqrt{y_qy_p}-\frac12\right),\quad E\ge E_{\mathrm{th}}. \] Both seed squeezing and signal modulation are charged to the same physical input budget. The manuscript gives the low-energy variational formula and the attaining covariances explicitly. 3. When should another channel receive photons? The one-channel capacity curves are increasing and concave. For strictly mixed environments, the optimal allocation equalizes marginal information gains: \[ C_j'(E_j^*)=\lambda\quad(E_j^*>0),\qquad C_j'(0+)\le\lambda\quad(E_j^*=0). \] A previously unused channel turns on when its initial information gain becomes competitive with the declining gain of the channels already in use. Pure-environment endpoints follow by continuity of the attained capacity. In the two-channel example in Figure 1, the second channel activates at total budget approximately \(E=0.436\) photons. The figures evaluate the analytic allocation law and display how photons divide between squeezing, modulation and different links. 4. A converse for the complete correlated input. A joint quadratic output-entropy support excludes all competing encodings. Its proof develops a sharp thermal-reference contraction using both Bogoliubov orientations and independently adjusted thermal references. The appendix supplies the regularized minimizer, Gibbs identity, full-state Hessian comparison, interpolation domains, residual propagation and limiting arguments. This connects a computable Gaussian transmitter design to a bound on every allowed quantum code. Use and scope. Communication theorists and optical-source designers can use measured loss and quadrature noise to allocate a common photon budget, choose the seed squeezing and modulation, identify inactive channels, and calculate an attained capacity benchmark for these memoryless channels. The all-energy result addresses the low-energy Holevo additivity question for a squeezed thermal attenuator, and extends it to heterogeneous finite products under one total budget. Version 1.0, 13 October 2026. The 16-page PDF contains the article, two vector figures, complete supplementary proofs and references.

title: Metadata about AI-generated stories: expert, human annotation relating to conflict, character gender and profession
abstract: This dataset contains 416 human annotations of AI-generated stories. Each row records a story identifier and observations about the story's protagonist, potential opponent, supporting character, and types of conflict, including violent, non-violent, and internal conflict. It also records whether the protagonist responds actively or passively to conflict, along with narrative descriptions and optional annotator notes.

title: Метод аналізу семантичної динаміки діалогів із формуванням пояснення результатів у цифрових сервісах психологічної підтримки
abstract: У статті розглянуто задачу аналізу семантичної динаміки діалогів у цифрових сервісах психологічної підтримки населення.Актуальність дослідження зумовлена тим, що зміст діалогу формується не лише окремими репліками, а й послідовністю станів, тематичних переходів, емоційних змін, комунікативних намірів і контекстних зв'язків між повідомленнями.Метою роботи є розроблення методу аналізу семантичної динаміки діалогів із формуванням пояснення результатів на основі графово-контекстного представлення.Запропонований метод подає діалог як траєкторію смислових станів, побудовану на основі семантичних профілів реплік, типізованих зв'язків графа, локальних фрагментів діалогу та матриці переходів між станами.У межах методу формалізовано показники тематичної та емоційної зміни, узгодженості переходу, подібності траєкторій станів, а також правила виявлення динамічних ситуацій: узгодженого розвитку, зміни теми, повторення станів, відсутності просування та ескалаційного фрагмента.Для інтерпретації результату формується пояснювальний підграф, який містить найбільш значущі репліки, теми, емоційні маркери, комунікативні наміри, стани та зв'язки між ними.Експериментальне дослідження виконано на основі відкритого набору даних MentalChat16K.Із набору було сформовано вибірку з 720 діалогів і 4800 реплік.Порівняння з текстовими та лінійно-контекстними підходами показало, що графово-контекстна модель забезпечує значення TransitionAcc на рівні 0,78 і SeqSim на рівні 0,74.Додавання пояснювального механізму підвищило Fidelity з 0,16 до 0,24 та зменшило Compactness до 0,18.Отримані результати підтверджують доцільність використання запропонованого методу для автоматизованого аналізу розвитку діалогу та формування пояснюваних результатів у цифрових сервісах психологічної підтримки.

title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.

title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

title: Denoise X: Self-Supervised U-Net for Quantum Mottle Suppression in Chest Radiography
abstract: Deep learning for medical image restoration is often constrained by the need for paired training data. Acquiring perfectly registered clean-noisy radiographs in vivo is impractical due to patient motion and radiation-dose limits. To address this, we employ a self-supervised Noise2Noise paradigm that trains on independently corrupted observations without paired clean images. We propose Denoise X, a lightweight self-supervised U-Net model (7.79M parameters) for suppressing quantum mottle and electronic readout noise in low-dose chest radiographs. It is trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset (112,120 images) using a stochastic Poisson-Gaussian noise simulator. Zero-shot evaluation on the unseen Montgomery County dataset achieved a PSNR of 36.09 dB and SSIM of 0.8806, outperforming the Bilateral filter while preserving high-frequency anatomical details. Using patch-wise inference, Denoise X processes native-resolution chest radiographs in ~2.2 s per image on a Tesla P100 GPU. Cross-domain evaluation on the Shenzhen dataset achieved 36.44 dB PSNR and 0.9099 SSIM, showing strong generalization. For resource-constrained deployment, the model was converted into a 31.16 MB ONNX model for efficient CPU inference on non-DICOM images.

It is trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset (112,120 images) using a stochastic Poisson-Gaussian noise simulator. Zero-shot evaluation on the unseen Montgomery County dataset achieved a PSNR of 36.09 dB and SSIM of 0.8806, outperforming the Bilateral filter while preserving high-frequency anatomical details. Using patch-wise inference, Denoise X processes native-resolution chest radiographs in ~2.2 s per image on a Tesla P100 GPU. Cross-domain evaluation on the Shenzhen dataset achieved 36.44 dB PSNR and 0.9099 SSIM, showing strong generalization. For resource-constrained deployment, the model was converted into a 31.16 MB ONNX model for efficient CPU inference on non-DICOM images.

title: AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
abstract: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested.We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion-Action-World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 233 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define eight metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of five SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos3) required world-state change scores of 0.100-0.280 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states.

title: Beyond Black Boxes: Visual Grounding for Text Embeddings
abstract: In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch. Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.

title: Multimodal Fusion of RGB and Complementary Modalities for Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation adds an auxiliary sensing stream to RGB images (RGB-X), such as thermal, LiDAR, depth, event, polarization, or light field. This can improve robustness in poor lighting and under motion blur. But different sensors often produce features that do not match well, and fusion can become unstable. To alleviate these issues, we propose a bidirectional polarity-aware cross-modality fusion (BPCF) module that effectively captures complementary cues while enhancing feature alignment. We evaluate the framework on six modality pairings: RGB-Thermal, RGB-LiDAR, RGB-Depth, RGB-Event, RGB-Polarization, and RGB-Light Field. Our model achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on eight public datasets, including MFNet, KITTI-360, DELIVER, DDD17, DSEC, MCubeS, ZJU, and UrbanLF. The codes and trained models will be released upon acceptance.

title: Arithmetic by Machine Learning: Learning the Four Arithmetic Operations, Exponentiation and Logarithm with Small Perceptrons
abstract: We study whether the four basic arithmetic operations, exponentiation a^b and the logarithm log_a b can be realised by small perceptrons trained by gradient descent. For each operation a small network is designed so that an exact solution exists in its weight space. For the four arithmetic operations and the logarithm, we test whether training from random initial weights on input–output examples finds this solution; for exponentiation, we verify the exact representation and the numerical convergence of training guided toward the known weights.Addition and subtraction are learned by a single linear layer. Multiplication uses a hidden layer with square activation and converges to the polarization identity ab = ¼[(a+b)² − (a−b)²]. Division uses a logarithmic hidden layer and an exponential output with complex-valued forward computation. The logarithm uses a log-log hidden layer and converges to the exact solution with Adam. Exponentiation uses a sign-dependent log-type activation and a double-exponential output, representing a^b exactly for a, b > e; it reaches the exact weights only with an auxiliary loss toward them, so learning it from examples alone remains open.This report consolidates the author's own series of Qiita articles (2018–2026). The square-activation multiplication network (2018) and the complex-valued division network (January 2020) were developed independently of, and published before, Neural Arithmetic Logic Units (2018) and Neural Power Units (2020), respectively.

title: RIDI-PREDICT-v1: generation archive and post-run analysis recovery (Supplementary Data 4)
abstract: Supplementary Data 4 for the RIDI study, “Identical evaluation scores conceal which questions language models answer correctly”. This archive contains the RIDI-PREDICT-v1 frozen study materials, per-question generation records for all 24 planned model-by-benchmark-by-draw units, original failed analysis and diagnostic records, and the dated post-run analysis-recovery amendment, derivative script, results and verification receipts. title: Exploration or exploitation? The double-edged effects of AI use modes on radical creativity: evidence from AI-enabled drug discovery
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

title: A multidimensional knowledge tracing hybrid model integrating semantics and dialogue behavior for cultural education
abstract: In intelligent dialogue systems for cultural teaching, traditional knowledge tracing models exhibit a limited capacity to interpret open-ended responses and struggle to characterize multidimensional cultural learning abilities or to effectively leverage the structural information embedded in instructional dialogues. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an improved SAINT+ (Separated Self-Attentive Neural Knowledge Tracing)–DKVMN (Dynamic Key-Value Memory Network) hybrid knowledge tracing model tailored for cultural teaching. The core idea is to introduce semantic–dialogue–ability structural constraints at both the sequence modeling and memory modeling levels simultaneously. Specifically, the model unifies the semantic information of students' open-ended responses—encoded via RoBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach)—with dialogue-behavior features into structured learning events, thereby incorporating the dialogue process into sequence modeling. At the memory layer, the conventional single-dimensional mastery probability is extended into multidimensional concept mastery states, capturing the evolution of distinct ability dimensions in cultural learning, including factual understanding, explanatory ability, reflective depth, and confidence. The traceability of state transitions is further enhanced through an update mechanism constrained by behavioral conditions. Building on these components, the model achieves a balance between predictive performance and interpretability through joint multi-task training. Experimental results show that the proposed model attains an overall prediction accuracy of 0.862 (95% CI 0.856, 0.868) and an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.905 (95% CI 0.899, 0.912). For the rubric classification of open-ended responses, the overall accuracy reaches approximately 0.877, with RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) values ranging from 0.09 to 0.11 across all ability dimensions. Moreover, the designed attention and memory-writing visualizations provide teachers with traceable concept-level evidence of student learning. Overall, the experiments demonstrate that the proposed model offers strong effectiveness and interpretability in intelligent dialogue systems for cultural teaching, providing reliable technical support for intelligent tutoring systems aimed at cultivating complex cultural competencies.

title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($ρ^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.

title: OpenMQPI: An MLIR-based Pipeline to Offload Quantum Circuits via OpenMP
abstract: Quantum computing introduces specialized software stacks and programming interfaces that are often tightly coupled to specific ecosystems and hardware backends, limiting interoperability and software reuse. For HPCQC application developers, this complicates the integration of quantum accelerators into existing applications. Existing quantum frameworks also use ecosystem-specific circuit representations and compilation pipelines, hindering integration with established heterogeneous compiler infrastructures. We propose OpenMQPI, an MLIR-based OpenMP extension for quantum programming that leverages OpenMP's standardized target offloading infrastructure to integrate quantum resources into HPC applications. OpenMQPI introduces QPIR, a lightweight MLIR dialect for representing quantum circuits within OpenMP target regions, and a compiler pipeline that performs quantum-specific optimizations and lowers circuits to executables compatible with OpenMP offloading. At runtime, an MQSS plugin enables the generated executable to offload quantum circuits to quantum hardware through the OpenMP target offloading model. We evaluate OpenMQPI using the VQE, QFT, and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms with 5, 10, 15, and 20 qubits, comparing execution times against Qiskit and CUDA Quantum. OpenMQPI achieves the lowest average VQE execution time across all tested qubit configurations. At 20 qubits, it requires 5.18 s, compared with 5.83 s for Qiskit and 7.39 s for CUDA Quantum. For QFT and Deutsch-Jozsa, OpenMQPI achieves execution times comparable to Qiskit and lower than those of CUDA Quantum.

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

title: PLEDGE: Progressive Lossy Error-Bounded Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) codecs report reconstruction quality after compression, and give users little control over the distortion of individual primitives. We present PLEDGE, a training-free, progressive, error-bounded codec that translates four user-declared tolerances into per-primitive quantization bounds: screen-space position, footprint deformation due to rotation and scale, view-dependent color, and opacity. The bounds apply throughout a declared camera domain, including previously unseen viewpoints. Position and opacity are bounded directly; footprint deformation is bounded under the rasterizer's affine projection model, and color is bounded over all viewing directions. PLEDGE organizes quantized residuals into a progressive bitstream with explicit error bounds for every valid prefix. Experiments across thirteen scenes verify all declared per-mechanism bounds and demonstrate competitive rate-distortion performance. The four tolerances incur substantially different rate costs, so users can spend rate where their application needs it.

Position and opacity are bounded directly; footprint deformation is bounded under the rasterizer's affine projection model, and color is bounded over all viewing directions. PLEDGE organizes quantized residuals into a progressive bitstream with explicit error bounds for every valid prefix. Experiments across thirteen scenes verify all declared per-mechanism bounds and demonstrate competitive rate-distortion performance. The four tolerances incur substantially different rate costs, so users can spend rate where their application needs it.

abstract: Source code and full-precision per-image results for the article "Joint Refinement of Center of Gravity Thresholds for Color Quantization: Gains and Limits of Separable Color Partitions", submitted to Computer Vision and Image Understanding. title: Jethro Hierarchical Multi-Agent Orchestration: A Scalable 10-50-100-1000 Delegation Control Plane with Hard Scoped Budgets for Autonomous Enterprises
abstract: As enterprises transition from single-turn Large Language Model (LLM) assistants to large-scale multi-agent swarms, flat peer-to-peer and centralized star topologies suffer from severe coordination bottlenecks, exponential O(N^2) communication overhead, context window degradation, and unconstrained API token expenditure. Drawing inspiration from the classical Jethro organizational principle of tiered delegation (groups of 10, 50, 100, and 1000), this paper introduces the Jethro Hierarchical Multi-Agent Orchestration (JHMO) architecture. JHMO establishes a deterministic 4-tier enterprise control plane comprising: (1) Tier-10 Tactical Execution Squads, (2) Tier-50 Domain Supervisors (Maker-Checker verification gates), (3) Tier-100 Departmental Orchestrators, and (4) Tier-1000 Executive Control Plane with hard scoped budget circuit breakers and Human-in-the-Loop board gating. Empirical benchmarks demonstrate a 98.1% reduction in redundant context tokens and 99.6% task completion fidelity.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Kazakh-Language Educational Assistants: Sentiment Classification and Question Answering with and Without Context
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.

title: Annotated Food Recipe Dataset for Allergen Identification Using Natural Language Processing Techniques
abstract: This dataset contains annotated Indonesian recipe texts for allergen identification and Named Entity Recognition (NER) tasks. The dataset was constructed from Indonesian food recipes and consists of token-level annotations containing word sequences, Part-of-Speech (POS) tags, and allergen entity labels. Each sentence in the dataset is segmented into individual tokens and annotated using the BIO tagging scheme to identify allergen-related entities. The dataset provides linguistic information through POS tagging, which can be utilized as additional features for natural language processing models, particularly for allergen detection, information extraction, and NER-based applications in the culinary domain. The dataset contains 24,000 annotated tokens extracted from Indonesian recipes. Each record includes four attributes: 1. Recipe #: Identifier of the recipe source. 2. Word: Individual token or word extracted from the recipe text. 3. POS: Part-of-Speech category assigned to each token. 4. Tag: BIO annotation label representing allergen-related entities. This dataset supports research in Indonesian Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially for developing and evaluating machine learning and deep learning models for food allergen recognition.

title: When AI ads violate expectations: the interplay of AI character, product type, and advertising appeal of AI ads on consumer attitudes
abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping video advertising production. Using expectancy violations theory as an interpretive lens, this study develops a framework in which ad appeal (rational vs. emotional), product type (high-tech vs. low-tech), and AI character embodiment (no character vs. animal-like vs. human-like) jointly relate to ad attitude and to two appraisals: perceived novelty and perceived uncanniness. This study tests the framework in five between-subjects experiments with consumers recruited from an online panel. Results show that rational appeals outperform emotional appeals in AI-generated ads, especially for low-tech products. Novelty is positively and uncanniness negatively associated with ad attitude, and the indirect effects through both appraisals are consistent with the proposed process. Human-like AI characters amplify uncanniness in emotional low-tech executions. In one rational low-tech execution, an animal-like character lowered uncanniness relative to a no-character baseline, but ad attitude did not differ significantly. The findings extend expectancy-violation theorizing in AI advertising and offer configuration-level design guidance for brands deploying disclosed AI-generated advertising.

title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.

title: Unbalanced W-Flow: Unbalanced Wasserstein Drifting under Finite-Batch Marginal Fluctuations
abstract: Teacher-free one-step generative models such as W-Flow learn directly from distributional objectives, with the Sinkhorn divergence providing the strongest empirical performance among the energies studied in W-Flow. However, Sinkhorn divergence is based on balanced optimal transport, whose exact marginal constraints can induce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. We introduce UW-Flow, which replaces the balanced Sinkhorn energy with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity. The resulting dynamics retain W-Flow's cross-minus-self structure, recover the balanced limit, and preserve target identifiability under suitable assumptions. We further characterize the finite-batch velocity error of balanced and unbalanced transport by comparing each minibatch field with its population counterpart. Our analysis identifies conditions under which marginal relaxation yields smaller minibatch-to-population velocity error, and shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation while the corresponding Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) sensitivity remains controlled by local transport geometry. Controlled experiments on fixed-support and continuous two-mode distributions support these predictions. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100, UW-Flow improves generation under matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation and consistent improvements in the class-conditional setting.

title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.

title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
abstract: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.

title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
abstract: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it is almost immune to self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, essentially the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $28\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes twelve times as long to build, and about as fast as those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and still has faster queries. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 48-core machine it is almost three times faster than that of PHast+. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive a lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on this fraction, and we estimate that the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about one tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

title: MHVF: Training-Free GUI Grounding via Verification-Guided Multi-Hypothesis Search
abstract: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views. Verification scores then guide a second round of local search and rank candidates retained from both search levels for final selection. Experiments with five general-purpose and GUI-specific models across eight benchmark settings demonstrate improvements in grounding accuracy in most settings. MHVF improves UI-Venus-Ground-7B by 4.3 and 2.1 percentage points on Mind2Web and VisualWebBench, respectively, and raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro from 23.6% to 53.6%.

title: Documented, accepted, honoured: an audit of decoding parameters on a hosted LLM inference API
abstract: Benchmark results for hosted language models are reported with a decoding configuration (a temperature, a nucleus threshold, sometimes a seed) on the assumption that the provider applies what the request asks for. We test that assumption on one provider, Fireworks AI, for all 18 chat models in its serverless catalogue and every sampling parameter its API reference documents. For each (model, parameter) we separate three facts: what the reference documents, whether the API accepts the parameter, and whether the output distribution responds to it, which we call honoured. The last is decided by a two-sample permutation test on 10 to 40 completions per setting across four prompts, with a positive control that estimates the test's power and a negative control on 37 pairs of identical arms. The API accepts every documented parameter on every model. Of 144 cells for the eight parameters that shape the sampling distribution, 104 show an effect. Five show none although the test had power against a greedy-strength effect and the data exclude an effect as large as the weakest one the parameter has where it works: mirostat on four models and typical_p on one. Mirostat is honoured on six other models behind the same API, so whether it takes effect depends on the model. The API also accepts four parameters it does not document. Two change nothing we can detect, and ignore_eos works and returns raw control tokens. At temperature 0 one model in 18 returns byte-identical text to ten identical concurrent requests, and two do when the requests are sent one at a time. A fixed seed, documented as "Random seed for deterministic sampling", does not raise temperature-0 agreement (permutation p = 0.52). We release the instrument, the completions behind every parameter verdict, and the collection date of every result.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking Data
abstract: Overview This repository contains the complete data generated from executing a suite of benchmarks on multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) from different hardware providers and technologies. It includes the raw and processed results, and also every quantum circuit, compilation/transpilation setting and execution configuration used. With these, every experiment can be fully reproduced, audited, or re-run on other devices. Its aim is to provide an open, transparent and reproducible basis for comparing the performance of current quantum hardware. Current contents (version [1.0.0]) This version contains the data for the following benchmark: [ghz-benchmarking.zip] (Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services): This version contains the data from benchmarking ten commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of GHZ states via direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state compatible with the genuine multipartite entanglement threshold F = 1/2. All experiments were run through the providers’ cloud services, using each provider’s default compilation and no error mitigation, so the results reflect the performance experienced by end users. File structure Each benchmark is provided as a separate ZIP archive ([benchmark_name].zip). A README.md file in each ZIP describes the formats, naming conventions and data schema for each benchmark. Future versions This is a living dataset. Data from additional benchmarks run on the same and on further devices will be added in future versions of this record. How to cite If you use this dataset, please cite [the associated paper: Authors, Title, arXiv:XXXX.XXXXX] and this dataset. Cite the version-specific DOI to reference the exact data you used, or the concept DOI to reference the dataset as a whole. Acknowledgements

title: CHIMA: Design and Evaluation of a Lightweight Cryptographic System for IoT Applications
abstract: Resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices motivate the investigation into cryptographic designs with measurable implementation costs. This work presents CHIMA (Cryptography cHaotic lIghtweight systeM and Authentication), an experimental system combining a key generator based on chaotic states, a Feistel cipher using the AES substitution box and a keyed bit permutation, and a Lesamnta-LW-based ciphertext check. Logistic, H’enon, and Lorenz systems are examined for key generation, and cipher variants with 64-bit and 128-bit blocks are evaluated. The study reports functional tests, avalanche measurements, NIST statistical tests, and implementation measurements on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M33, and Cortex-M7 microcontrollers. Controlled WiFi/MQTT and LoRa experiments assess communication interoperability. The results show that the chaotic key generator achieved high entropy and passed all NIST statistical tests, indicating its suitability for generating pseudorandom sequences. Based on the combined encryption and decryption times, CHIMA-64 requires 57.95–64.16% less time than PRESENT, while CHIMA-128 requires 23.60–59.36% less time than AES-128 and 13.32–47, as well as 10% less time than CLEFIA across the three platforms.

title: Comparison of Internal Validation Strategies for Estimating Machine Learning Model Performance in One-Year Mortality Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abstract: Background: Machine learning (ML) performance estimates in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) may depend on internal validation strategy, especially in small datasets. Aim: To develop models for one-year mortality prediction and compare performance, calibration, decision-analytic performance, and uncertainty estimates using a conventional train–test split and nested cross-validation (nCV). Methods: We analyzed a public dataset of 165 patients with HCC, including 63 one-year deaths. Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and CatBoost were developed using fold-specific preprocessing, cost-sensitive learning, Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and training-based threshold selection. L2-penalized logistic regression provided a conventional benchmark. Models were evaluated using a stratified 80/20 split and five-fold nCV with five inner folds. Six stratified splits assessed partition variability, and unweighted models assessed the effect of class weighting. Discrimination, threshold-dependent classification, calibration, and decision-analytic performance were assessed using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, balanced accuracy, Matthew’s correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration curves, and decision-curve analysis. Confidence intervals used 2000 bootstrap resamples; SHAP was used for interpretation. Results: In the conventional split, RF and CatBoost achieved the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.892 each), while RF achieved the highest PR-AUC (0.860). Under nCV, RF had the highest mean outer-fold ROC-AUC (0.788) and pooled out-of-fold ROC-AUC (0.784). XGBoost had the highest mean PR-AUC (0.673), whereas CatBoost had the highest pooled PR-AUC (0.648). RF had the lowest mean Brier score (0.188), followed by XGBoost (0.194) and CatBoost (0.203). Calibration varied across models, with pooled calibration slopes of 1.438, 0.691, and 0.427, respectively. Across six 80/20 splits, mean ROC-AUC values were 0.792, 0.769, and 0.761 for RF, XGBoost, and CatBoost, respectively, with substantial partition-dependent variation. Removing class weighting yielded broadly comparable performance. Bootstrap confidence intervals were narrower for pooled nCV predictions, but the evaluation samples differed in size (165 versus 33 patients), precluding attribution of this difference to validation strategy alone. Decision-curve analysis was exploratory because no clinically actionable threshold was prespecified. SHAP identified AFP, ALP, hemoglobin, albumin, performance status, and AST among the most influential RF predictors; the highest-ranked predictors were generally consistent across outer folds. Conclusions: nCV separated model development from evaluation and reduced reliance on a single small test set. RF was selected by the prespecified mean outer-fold ROC-AUC criterion, but differences among tree-based models were small and no clear discrimination advantage over penalized logistic regression was demonstrated. External validation is needed before clinical use.

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Full classification of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard codes
abstract: The $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}^n$. A $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is a GH code over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ which is the Gray map image of a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive code. A recursive construction gives such codes $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$, of type $(n;t_1,\dots,t_s)$ and length $p^t$, and a partial classification of them is known. In this paper, we complete the classification of these codes for every prime $p$. The main tool is the derived code, obtained by puncturing the code outside a block of coordinates determined by its kernel. For a nonlinear code $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$ with $t_1\geq2$, the derived code is a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{s-1}}$-linear GH code of the same family, although the mechanism for odd $p$ differs from the binary one. As a consequence, for $t\geq3$, there are $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)$ nonequivalent such codes of length $p^t$ if $p$ is odd, and $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)-1$ if $p=2$, where $\mathcal P(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$. In particular, this completes the classification of the $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard codes. We also prove a conjecture on the codes with $t_1\geq2$ and $t_s=0$.

title: LegalRewardBench: Benchmarking Reward Models for Legal Preference Evaluation
abstract: Reward models are central to preference alignment for legal tasks, yet existing reward model benchmarks are still primarily centered on general-domain preferences. In this work, we introduce LegalRewardBench, the first human-verified benchmark for evaluating reward models in the legal domain. The benchmark organizes legal preference evaluation into five capability levels: knowledge, understanding, analysis, decision, and writing, and preference examples are constructed through rubric-guided automatic judging combined with human verification. We evaluate three families of judges, covering both general and fine-tuned models, and generative and discriminative architectures. Experimental results show that strong general-purpose generative models are currently the most robust legal reward models, while existing fine-tuned reward models transfer less reliably to legal preference evaluation. We also conduct detailed comparisons of input organizations and training strategies.

title: Theory of Trotter Error with Variable-Weight Schedules
abstract: Trotterization is a widely used algorithm for simulating quantum evolutions and consists of approximating a target unitary through a local linear decomposition of its generator that is repeated over $N$ steps. We introduce {scheduled trotterization}, a variable-weight modification in which the coefficients of the local linear decomposition are allowed to change from step to step. Using the geometry of the Lie group of unitary operators, we express the global endpoint error as a product of transported local defects, whose leading terms are obtained by two applications of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, one inside each local step and one between different transported defects, separating the internal Trotter error from the external accumulation error. While we recover recent tighter bounds on the global approximation error when the weights are held fixed, the new framework allows us to propose a weight-varying schedule that significantly decreases the global error. For exact infinitesimal synthesis, we prove that this improves the usual fixed-weight $O(N^{-1})$ behavior to $O(N^{-2})$, without changing the basic pulse skeleton. We also extend the framework to imperfect infinitesimal synthesis, as arises in quantum gate synthesis problems, where admissible coefficients may only approximate the desired local corrections. In this case, the error is controlled by a local covering parameter measuring the quality of the available coefficient set. Numerical experiments for random $\SU(2)$ targets further support the predicted theoretical improvements. The results suggest a novel perspective for the analysis of Trotter errors, which can be treated as schedulable quantities to be coherently canceled at the endpoint.

title: Generalizable Representations for Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning
abstract: Multilingual models are essential in natural language processing (NLP), the field of enabling computational models to process and generate human language. These models are crucial for expanding information access across linguistic boundaries, with machine translation models being particularly central to this effort. However, with approximately 7,000 languages spoken worldwide, it is infeasible to acquire sufficient training data for every language. This data scarcity challenge highlights the importance of cross-lingual generalization, the ability to transfer knowledge learned from some languages to settings with little or no training data. Such generalization depends on a model's ability to learn internal representations that are shared and consistent across languages. While the \textit{classical} form of cross-lingual generalization involves training a model for a task in some languages and evaluating it on others, its application in machine translation is more complex as the input and output languages are inherently different. The directional nature of machine translation calls for \textit{compositional} generalization, which requires the model to combine knowledge from trained directions (e.g., English-to-German and German-to-French) to directly perform translation for unseen directions (e.g., English-to-French). Moreover, the pre-training fine-tuning paradigm introduces a crucial \textit{temporal} dimension to generalization. This perspective concerns how well a model's pre-trained capabilities are preserved after specializing on selected tasks or languages. This thesis addresses these three aspects of generalization: classical, compositional, and temporal. First, we investigate compositional generalization in translation models trained from scratch. We demonstrate that a primary reason why multilingual translation models fail to generalize compositionally is that their internal representations become highly entangled with information specific to the input language. We identify that this entanglement is reinforced by the residual connections within the model's architecture. By proposing a method that relaxes this structural constraint, we achieve substantial improvements on unseen translation directions. We then extend the investigation to the temporal dimension of generalization by incorporating pre-trained models. We observe that despite large-scale multilingual pre-training, a model's internal representations often remain highly specific to the input language. Moreover, when these models are specialized for particular translation directions, they are prone to catastrophic forgetting, which substantially degrades their existing capabilities. To counteract this, our work evaluates several established mitigation strategies from the literature and introduces a novel approach. Our proposed method produces a more interpretable view of the model's internal representations, although this benefit comes with a trade-off in translation quality. Our investigation then extends to large language models (LLMs), which operate as general-purpose instruction-following systems. For these models, which typically use a decoder-only architecture, we first identify the middle layers as the most effective positions for intervention. Building on this finding, we propose a modular and computationally efficient post-hoc method to enhance language invariance in the model's representations. This approach leads to substantial improvements in both classical cross-lingual transfer scenarios and the compositional generalization cases examined earlier. Lastly, we revisit classical cross-lingual transfer with a novel application for attribute-controlled machine translation. This method trains a classifier to distinguish text attributes in languages with available labeled data and then transfers this capability to guide translations for other languages lacking such resources. The approach operates on the model's internal activations rather than weights, making it suitable for scenarios where model weights must remain fully frozen. When compared to an oracle setup that updates the model weights, our activation-based method demonstrates stronger robustness against domain shifts. Each of the contributions above is situated within a model modification scope that aligns with evolving practices in the field, ranging from training models from scratch to performing post-hoc interventions on large pre-trained models. This thesis advances the development of multilingual NLP models that not only achieve strong performance under trained conditions but also acquire more generalizable and adaptable underlying representations.

Each of the contributions above is situated within a model modification scope that aligns with evolving practices in the field, ranging from training models from scratch to performing post-hoc interventions on large pre-trained models. This thesis advances the development of multilingual NLP models that not only achieve strong performance under trained conditions but also acquire more generalizable and adaptable underlying representations.

title: Künstliche Intelligenz – Chance oder Risiko? Vortrag beim Katholischen Bildungswerk Frankenburg am Hausruck
abstract: lides of a general-audience evening talk (about 90 minutes plus discussion), given inGerman at the Catholic adult-education centre (Katholisches Bildungswerk) inFrankenburg am Hausruck, Upper Austria, on 13 October 2026. The talk explains, without formulas, what artificial intelligence can and cannot dotoday. Part 1 shows where AI already sits in everyday life (timetables, weather,navigation, licence-plate recognition, recommendations). Part 2 covers data as the rawmaterial, from monastic tithe registers to social media, the planned Google datacentre in Kronstorf, and open government data. Part 3 demonstrates AI agents on threelive examples: analysing the Frankenburg municipal council minutes 2021–2026, planninga bicycle tour, and a study of Alpine pumped-hydro storage. Part 4 contrastsopportunities (retinal-image diagnostics) with risks: hallucination, deepfakes,accountability, military use. It closes with three take-home messages. Includes the video shown in the talk: an AI-agent-generated flood visualisation(Perschling valley, September 2024) together with the slide explaining its limits.Text and the author's own figures are CC BY 4.0; third-party images and screenshotsare credited on the final slide and excluded from the licence.

title: Anti-Dual Vector Foil G: Composite Algebra and Composite Fiber Accounting of Weight-Dependent Annihilation Operators
abstract: Skeleton-layer annihilation operators are divided by the readout level of theirdecision rules into three types: skeleton-dependent, order-dependent, and absolutevalue-dependent. This paper studies two problems for weight-dependent annihilation operators: composite algebra and composite fiber accounting. On the composite algebra side, the composition table of threshold rules and ranking rules satisfies four operator identities: threshold composition takes the maximum parameter,ranking composition takes the sum of parameters, and both cross-type compositionpaths collapse, on every fixed network, to an initial segment of the global lexicographic order, whose parameter is a counting function of network weights andindices. The semigroup generated by threshold atoms and ranking atoms is closedunder composition; the class of elementary weight-dependent rules strictly containsthis generated semigroup, but in the sense of a uniformly predicate-syntacticallyclosed class it is the smallest rule class containing the two generators and closedunder composition and predicate conversion. The semigroup verdict exhibits coordinate differentiation: the skeleton-dependent end is trivially closed, the orderdependent end is closed under parameter addition, the pure-threshold end is closedunder taking extremes, and cross-coordinate composition forces an enlargement ofthe generated class. The readout level under composition is the supremum of thecomponents. On the fiber accounting side, in the standard discrete weight-latticemodel, the fiber cardinality of a threshold operator is determined jointly by thenumber of missing edges and the threshold, while the fiber cardinality of a ranking operator is given by a product formula involving tied indicator elements, andon subdomains of distinct weights it reduces to a falling factorial; all are verifiedby deterministic exhaustive enumeration over the whole space. Composite fibersare precisely described by a fiber decomposition identity: when composed with aweight-layer bijection, the composite fiber is equinumerous with the single-operatorfiber; when composed with a general weight-layer operator, the composite fiber isno smaller than the weight-layer end, and if the weight-layer map is surjective ontoits range, then the composite fiber is also no smaller than the annihilation end. Thedifference between the two composition orders is priced in bits; in the single-objectmodel, one spanning element corresponds to exactly one bit, and the redistributionof tied adjudication rights is its mechanism.

title: A UC-Secure Protocol for Privacy-Preserving Preferential Voting with Verifiable Encrypted Ballots
abstract: Preferential voting allows participants to rank multiple alternatives according to their preferences rather than being restricted to selecting a single option. Such mechanisms are used in national and local elections and, in decentralized governance, can be applied to committee selection, the prioritization of protocol upgrades or funding applications, and the choice of an electricity supplier or energy source. Of particular practical interest are systems in which participants have different stakes and their voting weights are proportional to those stakes. In the model considered in this work, each voter submits a complete ranking of the alternatives. The key technical challenge is to verify that an encrypted ballot encodes a valid ranking, that is, that exactly one rank is assigned to each alternative and each rank is used exactly once, without revealing the voter’s preferences. We propose a UC-secure protocol for privacy-preserving preferential voting with verifiable encrypted ballots. A ranking is represented as a permutation matrix whose entries are encrypted using an additively homomorphic cryptosystem. To verify ballot validity, each encrypted row of the matrix is accompanied by a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that it is a unit vector. The encrypted rows are then homomorphically summed, and the resulting vector is checked against the all-ones vector. Together, these checks ensure that the encrypted matrix is a permutation matrix without revealing the ranking itself. Using an O(logm)-size unit-vector proof for each of the m rows yields O(mlogm) ballot-validity proof data, while the overall ballot size remains O(m2) because the encrypted matrix contains m2 ciphertexts. The protocol supports stake-weighted tallying and threshold decryption, so that only the final aggregate result is revealed. The UC security of the protocol is established in the random-oracle model under the Decisional Diffie–Hellman (DDH) assumption. The theoretical analysis shows that the computational complexity of generating and verifying a single ballot is O(m2) and that the ballot size is also O(m2), where m is the number of alternatives. The experimental results are consistent with this quadratic scaling: for 32 alternatives, the mean ballot-generation time is 87 ms, the mean verification time is 36 ms, and the reported cryptographic ballot payload is 106 KiB. These measurements indicate practical ballot-construction and verification costs for elections with a moderate number of alternatives.

title: TrackShield: An Efficient Runtime Defense Against Availability Attacks on High-Performance Real-Time Multi-Object Tracking
abstract: High-performance camera-based perception pipelines must sustain per-frame real-time budgets on resource-constrained embedded GPU platforms. Availability attacks such as SlowTrack inflate the persistent state of multi-object trackers: data-association workload accumulates across frames, so per-frame latency increases and drives the pipeline past its deadline. Detector- and NMS-layer defenses do not directly control this persistent tracker-side resource. We present TrackShield, a lightweight runtime resource-management layer that protects the tracker at the point where attack-induced workload accumulates. TrackShield combines low-overhead anomaly monitoring with staged birth capping, pruning of young or weakly matched tracks, and per-stage association-input admission control. Its hard admission guard provides a deterministic bound on admitted association workload, independently of the heuristic monitor. On a Jetson AGX Orin, TrackShield reduces attacked tracking-stage latency from $139.90$ to $6.27$\,ms and whole-pipeline P99 latency from $190.9$ to $48.8$\,ms, at a benign MOTA cost of $1.06$ points. As an availability defense, TrackShield focuses on keeping the tracker responsive under attack instead of recovering the full tracking accuracy degraded by adversarial detections.

title: Learning in Orbit: Onboard Training and Closed-Loop Attitude Control with a Thermal Segmentation Model on a Spacecraft
abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).

title: I2O2I-Nav: A Benchmark with a Modular Agent for Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor-to-Indoor Navigation
abstract: Service and delivery robots often need to complete long-horizon navigation missions spanning indoor and outdoor environments. Existing embodied navigation benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated stages or partial cross-domain journeys, providing limited support for assessing how heterogeneous navigation capabilities compose under continuous execution. We introduce I2O2I-Nav, a physics-enabled benchmark of 20 real-world composite scenes spanning over 115,000 square meters across multiple buildings and floors, with aligned 3DGS rendering and collision geometry. Its three-level evaluation progresses from independent primitives to two-stage compositions and complete four-stage I2O2I missions. Each stage starts from its predecessor's actual endpoint, while stage-conditional metrics track completion and localize failures along the mission. We further propose the MODULAR-Agent that coordinates frozen navigation policies through completion verification, stage handoffs, and bounded recovery. Evaluation across 1,374 episodes highlights the difficulty of continuous composition. The MODULAR-Agent achieves 40.5-76% success on individual primitives, but full I2O2I success remains low. Compared with a fixed policy chain using the same underlying policies, it more than doubles success on both Indoor-to-Outdoor (I2O) and Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I), while improving full-mission success from 1.15% to 4.02%. Stage-wise analysis shows that the MODULAR-Agent enables more missions to reach the final object-navigation stage, where conditional success remains low, revealing challenges in both long-horizon stage execution and completion decisions.

title: DexStitch: Learning and Composing Dexterous Skills from Human Videos via Contact-Aware Robotic Inpainting
abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.
